column6: The commentary treats "glorify the Name" as keeping it from misuse; Leviticus directly forbids profaning YHWH's holy Name and requires that it be sanctified among Israel.
Ezekiel's restoration turns on God vindicating and sanctifying the great Name Israel profaned among the nations, a concrete public counterpart to guarding the Name.
The psalm calls all creatures to praise YHWH's Name because that Name alone is exalted and its majesty is above earth and heaven, joining the commentary's Name and height.
Isaiah names God the high and lofty one whose Name is Holy, supplying a compact Hebrew Bible counterpart to "the Most High" and the purified Name.

column5: Name praised from sunrise to sunset
column6: The commentary distributes praise across the day; this verse makes the praise of YHWH's Name run from sunrise to sunset.

column5: YHWH high above, glory above heavens
column6: The psalm's high YHWH and glory above the heavens give a specific biblical pairing for the Lord's incomparable height.
The commentary distinguishes protecting the divine Name from merely uttering it; the commandment forbids bearing YHWH's Name for emptiness.
The Arabic ism in 87:1 is cognate with Hebrew šēm; at Moses' call God gives the enduring divine Name to be remembered through generations.
The commentary excludes rival claimants from the Name; YHWH says "this is my Name" and refuses to give his glory or praise to idols.
The commentary's no-rival reading of the Name meets Zechariah's eschatological formula that YHWH will be one and his Name one.
Isaiah asks whom God can be likened or made equal to, giving a direct biblical analogue to the commentary's no namesake, peer, or competitor.
The Arabic height root in al-a'la corresponds to Hebrew Elyon; Abraham invokes YHWH as God Most High, maker of heaven and earth.

column5: claim to be like the Most High
column6: The boast to ascend above the clouds and resemble Elyon is the self-exalting reversal of the commentary's insistence that the highest lordship cannot be seized.

column5: tower to heaven, make a name
column6: The builders seek a tower reaching heaven and a name for themselves, a concrete negative counterpart to a Name exalted by God rather than self-appropriated.
God promises to make Abraham's name great, sharpening the commentary's contrast between bestowed elevation and a ruler's self-exaltation.
The commentary's Moses is sent to Pharaoh; the call narrative likewise commissions Moses to bring Israel out of Egypt through Pharaoh.
Moses protests that he is slow of speech, the biblical narrative behind the commentary's request for an eased mission and opened speech.
God answers Moses by promising to be with his mouth and teach him what to speak, closely matching a messenger enabled before addressing others.
Aaron is made Moses' speaking partner and God promises instruction for both, paralleling the commentary's emphasis on Moses asking that his brother share the work.
Pharaoh's "Who is YHWH?" and refusal to obey make a biblical counterpart to the commentary's Pharaoh who rejects the lordship offered to him.

column5: Pharaoh exalts himself against the people
column6: The plague narrative explicitly charges Pharaoh with exalting himself against God's people, matching the commentary's analysis of oppressive elevation.
The later oracle has Pharaoh claim the Nile as his own creation, another biblical portrait of pharaonic self-appropriation of divine prerogative.
Herod receives the crowd's cry that his voice is a god's, supplying a precise Christian example of a ruler being placed in the divine position.
The immediate judgment of Herod for not giving glory to God gives the consequence that the preceding divine acclamation lacks.
The commentary treats tasbih as excluding child-attribution to God; John places God's giving of the only Son at the center of its proclamation.

column5: Mary, Jesus, and Son of God
column6: Luke calls the child born of Mary the Son of God, providing the New Testament's own coordinate for the Jesus-and-Mary issue raised in the commentary.

column5: the one Name and Father, Son, Spirit
column6: The baptismal command uses the singular Name for Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, a Christian Name formula that differs from the commentary's non-distribution of divine appellation.
Against the commentary's self-seizing Pharaoh, Christ does not treat equality with God as something to grasp, making humility integral to the later exaltation.
God highly exalts Jesus and grants the Name above every name; this closely meets the commentary's Name-and-height language while assigning it christologically.

column5: Jesus confessed Lord to God's glory
column6: The universal confession of Jesus Christ as Lord is explicitly for the glory of God the Father, a Christian allocation of lordship beside the commentary's rejection of rival lords.
Thomas addresses the risen Jesus as Lord and God, the clearest New Testament counterpoint to the commentary's treatment of creaturely claims to divinity.
Luke gives Mary a prayer that magnifies the Lord, rather than a self-exaltation, which is essential context for the commentary's Mary-and-divinity scene.
Mary rejoices in God her Savior; this neighboring claim makes her own orientation to God explicit in contrast with her being imagined as a deity.
The commentary calls rival divine names empty claims; Paul says an idol is nothing in the world and that there is no God except one.
Paul acknowledges the vocabulary of many so-called gods and lords, the exact plural field against which the commentary sets one true Lord.
Paul's one-God/one-Lord confession assigns "one Lord" to Jesus Christ, a sharply relevant Christian reconfiguration of the commentary's exclusive lordship.
The angel rejects John's prostration and commands worship of God, concretely enacting the commentary's return of worship from a creature to God.
The opening petition of the Lord's Prayer asks that the Father's Name be hallowed, a direct liturgical analogue to treating the Name as the object of sanctification.
Jesus' petition makes glorifying God's Name an explicit address to the Father, closely matching the commentary's imperative toward the Name.

column5: glorifying the Name, God alone holy
column6: The heavenly song asks who will not glorify God's Name and calls him alone holy, bringing together purity, worship, and unmatched divinity.
This eucharistic thanksgiving thanks the holy Father for his holy Name made to dwell in believers' hearts, an early Christian liturgical development of the Name motif.
The priestly blessing ends with God placing his Name on Israel; it gives a covenantal counterpart to the commentary's Name as a marking claim of belonging.
Isaiah imagines persons writing "YHWH's" on the hand and taking Israel's name, a close textual meeting of name, inscription, and owned identity.

column5: Lamb's and Father's Names on foreheads
column6: Revelation makes the brand image explicit: the redeemed bear both the Lamb's Name and the Father's Name on their foreheads.
The beast's mark and name control allegiance and commerce, a deliberate inverse to the commentary's claim that the divine Name must not be transferred to a false claimant.
The final vision joins seeing God's face with his Name written on servants' foreheads, a striking counterpart to the commentary's linked discussions of face, Name, and mark.
God brings living creatures to Adam so that Adam names them, the biblical scene most directly beside the commentary's Adam, names, and creaturely knowledge.
This midrash turns Genesis' animal naming into a test before angels: they cannot supply the names, while Adam can, making the commentary's angelic limitation an explicit Jewish interpretation.
The commentary's Yunus boards a ship while fleeing; the Hebrew story gives the same departure to Tarshish by sea.
The sailors cast lots to identify the cause of the storm, directly paralleling the commentary's shipboard lot that falls against Yunus.
In Hebrew WLC numbering this verse has the fish swallow Jonah, the direct counterpart to the commentary's prophet being engulfed rather than swimming free.

column5: prayer from the belly of Sheol
column6: Jonah cries to YHWH from the belly of Sheol; it is the biblical fish-belly prayer beside the commentary's self-accusing tasbih.
The fish expels Jonah onto dry land, giving the narrative rescue that the commentary says prevents permanent confinement in the depths.

column5: Jonah interpreted as the Son of Man's sign
column6: Jesus rereads Jonah's three days in the sea creature as the Son of Man's three days in the heart of the earth, changing the story's later Christian meaning.

column5: bowing and kneeling before the Maker
column6: The psalm commands bodily bowing and kneeling before YHWH the Maker, a direct analogue to the commentary's tesbih joined to prostration and createdness.

column5: inner self blesses the holy Name
column6: The whole inner self blesses YHWH and his holy Name, matching the commentary's claim that praise is carried through inward disposition as well as speech.
The seraphim proclaim God's holiness and filling glory, a biblical heavenly liturgy for the commentary's purification and universal praise.
The living creatures offer unceasing holy praise to the Lord God, a Christian visionary counterpart to continuous heavenly tesbih.
The psalm summons sun, moon, and stars to praise YHWH, placing the commentary's moving heavenly bodies within a scriptural cosmic praise.
Flying birds join beasts and other creatures in praise, a concrete counterpart to the commentary's birds spread in the air within their own praise and prayer.

column5: every creature praises God and the Lamb
column6: Every creature in heaven, earth, under earth, and sea gives blessing to the enthroned God and the Lamb, extending the commentary's cosmic praise in a distinctively Christian direction.
The psalmist rises before dawn to cry out and hope in God's word, a specific biblical rhythm beside the commentary's daytime labor and night or dawn remembrance.
The psalmist's eyes anticipate the night watches to meditate on God's word, directly pairing night wakefulness with received speech.
Isaiah joins high heaven, creation, and naming: God brings out the host by number and calls every star by name, so none is missing.
The creator measures waters and marks out the heavens, a close biblical parallel to the commentary's Lord who creates, proportions, and guides.

column5: creator who formed and established earth
column6: Isaiah identifies YHWH as the creator who formed, fashioned, and established the earth, a specific analogue to the surah's ordered creation sequence developed under Rabb.
God's hand founded earth and spread heaven, and when he calls them they stand together, a concrete counterpart to the commentary's sustaining of what might otherwise slip away.

column5: all things hold together in Christ
column6: The commentary assigns cosmic holding to the Lord; Colossians says all things hold together in Christ, a Christian christological allocation of that sustaining work.
The heavens are stretched out like a tent, providing a biblical image for the commentary's sky as elevated roof or covering.

column5: heavens spread as a dwelling tent
column6: Isaiah describes God above the circle of earth stretching out heavens like a tent to dwell in, joining height, canopy, and divine transcendence.

column5: rain makes earth bud and yield
column6: Rain and snow descend, water the earth, and make it bud with seed and bread; this closely matches the commentary's cloud-to-rain-to-vegetation sequence.
The promised rain yields grass in the field for cattle, directly meeting the commentary's pasture, herd, and divine care imagery.

column5: grass for livestock and plants for people
column6: YHWH causes grass to grow for livestock and plants for human use, a precise biblical parallel to the commentary's pasture produced and sustained by the Lord.
The Lord is my shepherd gives the most direct Hebrew Bible counterpart to the commentary's Rabb as owner, guide, and shepherd of a flock.

column5: God feeds and rests the flock
column6: God himself promises to shepherd, feed, and give rest to his sheep, extending the commentary's care-and-guidance meaning of Rabb.
The Lord disciplines Israel as a parent disciplines a child, giving a biblical form to the commentary's non-biological nurturing and formation.

column5: the good shepherd lays down his life
column6: Jesus calls himself the good shepherd who lays down his life for the sheep, a Christian deployment of the shepherd-lord image central to the commentary's Rabb discussion.
The psalm credits God with forming inward parts and knitting a person in the womb, a biblical counterpart to the commentary's creator who brings bodies into ordered form.
The lot is cast in the lap but its every decision is from YHWH, a focused biblical companion to the commentary's lots, measured shares, and divine direction.

column5: God's Name in the sent messenger
column6: God tells Israel to heed the messenger because God's Name is in him; it is a striking biblical case where the Name accompanies a commissioned agent without becoming the agent's possession.
Jesus says he manifested the Father's Name to those given to him; it makes Name-bearing mission central to Christian theology in a way that invites comparison with the commissioned addressee of 87:1.

column5: God of gods and Lord of lords
column6: Deuteronomy calls YHWH God of gods and Lord of lords, a biblical superlative for the commentary's unshared lordship.

column5: King of kings and Lord of lords on Jesus
column6: Revelation places the title King of kings and Lord of lords on the returning Jesus, a further Christian assignment of supreme lordship beside the commentary's exclusivity claim.
Solomon asks that God's eyes remain on the house where God said his Name would be, making the Name a concentrated locus of prayer rather than a mere label.

column5: the place for God's Name to dwell
column6: Israel is to seek the place YHWH chooses to put his Name, a concrete cultic form of the commentary's claim that the Name is guarded and invoked.

column5: writing and sealing in a king's name
column6: A decree written in the king's name and sealed with his ring bears binding authority, supplying the legal-letter analogue to the commentary's image of a name at a letter's head.

column5: Come, let us go up to YHWH
column6: Isaiah's nations invite one another to go up to YHWH's mountain to receive instruction, a concrete Hebrew counterpart to the commentary's ascent-laden call to come.

column5: Joseph made lord over Pharaoh's house
column6: The Joseph story describes a human lordship over Pharaoh's house and Egypt granted by God, clarifying the commentary's observation that lord-language can have a human courtly use.

column5: one teacher and all are brothers
column6: Jesus forbids status-seeking religious titles by saying the disciples have one teacher and are brothers, a Christian warning adjacent to the commentary's refusal to elevate human religious figures into lords.

column5: statutes of heaven and rule on earth
column6: God's question about the ordinances of heaven and their rule on earth gives a biblical form to the commentary's ordered, sustained movements of the sky.
Ezekiel's mark identifies those who grieve over Jerusalem's evil; although it is not called the Name, it sharpens the commentary's bodily brand and distinguishing-sign image.
This expanded Jewish retelling develops Jonah's confinement in the fish and his penitential turn, a later interpretive companion to the commentary's rescue-through-confession reading.
The opening mishnah fixes the evening and morning times for reciting the Shema, a Jewish liturgical counterpart to praise and remembrance ordered across the day.
The Didache instructs believers to pray the Lord's Prayer three times daily, a concrete early Christian counterpart to the commentary's recurrent remembrance.
The Father's discipline is for believers' good so that they share holiness, a specific Christian counterpart to Rabb as gradual formation toward completion.
Moses compares his teaching and speech to rain and dew on tender grass, a close meeting of the commentary's commissioned speech with its cloud-to-pasture imagery.
Moses declares that he will proclaim YHWH's Name and calls hearers to ascribe greatness to God, an exceptionally direct biblical formulation beside the imperative of 87:1.

column5: YHWH descends and proclaims the Name
column6: In the cloud on Sinai, YHWH descends, stands with Moses, and proclaims the Name, joining the commentary's Moses mission, Name, and cloud imagery.

column5: the Name declared through divine attributes
column6: The divine Name is proclaimed with merciful, gracious, patient, and faithful attributes, clarifying how a Name can be guarded by true predication rather than empty use.

column5: no one like YHWH, majestic in holiness
column6: Moses' victory song asks who is like YHWH among gods and calls him majestic in holiness and praise, a direct counterpart to the commentary's no-peer tesbih.

column5: glory due the Name and worship
column6: The psalm couples giving YHWH the glory due his Name with worship, concretely joining the commentary's Name-object with praise enacted bodily.

column5: glory of the Name and offering
column6: Ascribing glory to YHWH's Name is followed by bringing an offering, a biblical instance of the commentary's claim that praise reaches beyond words into religious action.
The congregation is called to praise YHWH's great and awesome Name because he is holy, a compact Hebrew liturgical parallel to purity and exaltation of the Name.

column5: great Name and pure offering among nations
column6: Malachi joins YHWH's great Name among the nations to a pure offering, giving a prophetic counterpart to the commentary's protected Name and worship.

column5: nations' god-names and walking in YHWH's Name
column6: Micah contrasts peoples walking in their gods' names with Israel walking in YHWH's Name forever, closely matching the commentary's rejection of names distributed to rivals.

column5: El Shaddai and the Name YHWH
column6: The differentiated disclosure of El Shaddai and YHWH is a concrete biblical case for considering several divine appellations and their one divine referent.

column5: human pride brought low, YHWH alone exalted
column6: Isaiah contrasts lowered human loftiness with YHWH alone being exalted, directly sharpening the commentary's distinction between rightful height and arrogant self-elevation.
The prophetic voice calls human flesh grass, providing the opening term for the commentary's later pasture-and-fading sequence.
The grass withers and flower fades under God's breath, a precise textual companion to the surah's pasture that turns dark and perishes.

column5: grass fades but God's word stands
column6: The contrast between fading grass and God's enduring word closely joins the commentary's perishing pasture to its recipient who is taught and does not forget.
Jeremiah asks whether the nations' false gods or the heavens can give rain, then confesses dependence on YHWH; it joins empty rival names to rain and fertility.

column5: sign on hand, remembrance in the mouth
column6: The exodus memorial is a sign on hand and before the eyes so that YHWH's instruction remains in the mouth, a concrete parallel to the commentary's brand, remembrance, and spoken worship.
The psalm identifies YHWH as maker and owner, with worshipers his people and sheep of his pasture, gathering several of the commentary's Rabb images in one verse.
Hosea portrays God teaching Ephraim to walk and taking the child in his arms, a vivid Hebrew Bible form of the commentary's gradual nurturing and guidance.
Jonah's fish-belly prayer turns to thanksgiving and declares salvation belongs to YHWH, a distinct continuation beside the commentary's confession that clears God and locates fault in the prophet.
The Ninevites repent at Jonah's preaching, and Jesus calls himself greater than Jonah; this supplies the teaching-and-reminder outcome beyond the fish episode.

column5: Jonah as a sign to Nineveh
column6: Luke's Jesus makes Jonah himself a sign to Nineveh and the Son of Man a sign to his generation, a distinct Christian rereading from Matthew's three-days comparison.

column5: salvation in the Name of Jesus
column6: Acts locates salvation in the Name of Jesus given among humans, a Christian assignment of saving Name-language that stands beside the commentary's exclusive Name theology.
The Son inherits a Name more excellent than the angels, a Christian high-name claim especially relevant to the commentary's Name, height, and angelic knowledge discussion.

column5: an easy yoke and light burden
column6: Jesus calls his yoke easy and burden light, a close New Testament analogue to the commentary's repeated ease given to a commissioned servant.
Paul describes God as giving rain from heaven, fruitful seasons, food, and gladness, a Christian missionary statement beside the commentary's divine provision from sky to vegetation.

column5: grass clothed today and gone tomorrow
column6: Jesus invokes field grass alive today and destined for the oven tomorrow, a direct New Testament use of the commentary's transitory-pasture image.

column5: all flesh like grass, grass withers
column6: First Peter quotes the grass-and-flower fading formula, extending the commentary's fading-pasture image to mortal human life.

column5: the Lord our God is one
column6: Jesus recites Israel's one-God confession, giving a direct New Testament affirmation of the unshared lordship that frames the commentary.

column5: God's Name and Christ's new Name written on the victor
column6: The conqueror receives God's Name, the new Jerusalem's name, and Christ's new name; this extends the commentary's brand-and-name image in a distinctive Christian configuration.

God makes Moses elohim to Pharaoh and Aaron his prophet; this representative use supplies a nuanced biblical counterpoint to the commentary's contrast between Moses' true Lord and Pharaoh's self-deification.

column5: the Father's Name given to Jesus
column6: Jesus asks the Holy Father to keep his followers in the Father's Name "which you have given me," a specific continuation of the Christian Name-sharing claim.

column5: the good Name invoked over believers
column6: James speaks of the good Name invoked over believers, a New Testament instance of a Name placed upon persons that complements the commentary's mark-and-belonging image.

column5: human masters and the Master in heaven
column6: Ephesians distinguishes earthly masters from the shared Master in heaven, a Christian clarification of the commentary's human-master and divine-Lord semantic field.

column5: heaven and highest heaven cannot contain God
column6: Solomon says not even heaven and the highest heaven can contain God, a specific biblical check on spatial height alongside the commentary's Most High and heavenly roof images.
Jesus states that self-exalters will be humbled and the humble exalted, a direct ethical articulation of the commentary's good and bad forms of elevation.
Jewish tradition treats pronouncing the Name by its letters as a grave matter, an interpretive extension of the commentary's concern to protect the Name from misuse.
This mishnah is remembered as distinguishing the Temple's written pronunciation of the Name from a substituted provincial form; verify the exact subsection and wording before relying on it.
